text: Every circuit you've built so far has been a plan on paper. qiskit_aer's AerSimulator is where that plan actually runs — the standard local, high-performance backend for executing circuits without touching real quantum hardware, and the one you'll reach for in almost every lesson from here forward.

AerSimulator doesn't just run one algorithm internally. Automatic, the default, inspects your circuit and picks the fastest valid method itself. Statevector tracks the full complex amplitude vector exactly, but doubles in cost with every added qubit. Density_matrix handles mixed states under noise, stabilizer efficiently handles Clifford-only circuits, and matrix_product_state exploits limited entanglement in certain large, sparse circuits. You won't need to hand-pick a method for most circuits in this course, but knowing they exist matters once qubit counts climb.

Qiskit removed the old execute convenience function. The current pattern is explicit: transpile the circuit for your target backend, then call run directly. On AerSimulator, transpile is mostly a no-op for simple circuits, but it's good habit to always transpile, since the same code then works unchanged against real hardware.

get_counts returns a dictionary mapping each observed bitstring to how many shots produced it. For the Bell-state circuit, the only two possible outcomes are 00 and 11. A real seeded run at 1024 shots gives something like 00: 503, 11: 521, with 01 and 10 at exactly zero. That's not a perfect 512-512 split, even though the underlying probability is exactly 50/50 — ordinary sampling noise, not a bug or hardware error.

The next few lessons dig into exactly why that gap exists. First up: the difference between an exact statevector, which is ground truth, and a shot-based result, which is only ever an estimate of it — even on a perfectly noiseless simulator.
